definition.text: A theory that explains how, why and how fast new ideas and technologies spread through a social system.

facts.text: Everett Rogers popularised the theory in 1962, describing diffusion as an innovation being communicated through channels over time among members of a social system.
Study of diffusion took off in 1920s and 1930s rural sociology, which examined how independent US farmers adopted hybrid seeds, equipment and techniques.
The unit of adoption is usually an individual but can be an organization, a network cluster or a country; diffusion follows a five-step decision process.
Rate of adoption is the time a share of a social system takes to adopt; Rogers sorted adopters into five categories by innovativeness, and uptake follows an S curve over time.
Diffusion can fail to approach full adoption because of weaknesses, rival innovations or lack of awareness, or be widely taken up in some clusters but not others.
Adoption can have public consequences for others and private ones for the adopter, benefits and costs, and unintended negative effects.
The model predicts growth to a saturation level then decline, but cannot say how long it takes or what the saturation level will be.

definition.text: An agreement or secret cooperation among firms or individuals to limit competition, for example by dividing a market, fixing prices or limiting output.

facts.text: Collusion often arises in oligopolies, and price fixing harms consumers, so it is illegal under antitrust law and participants keep it secret; tacit collusion is considered legal.
A collusive price is unsustainable in a one-off game because members have an incentive to deviate; it needs repeated interaction and firms that value future profits.
With n symmetric firms, the cartel is stable only if the discount factor is at least (n-1)/n, so more firms make collusion harder to sustain.
Barriers include many firms, cost and demand differences, and asymmetric information; high concentration, homogeneous products and stable demand or excess capacity favour it.
Governments respond with fines and imprisonment, screening markets for suspicious pricing, and leniency for the first firm to confess.
In 2019 the European Commission found BMW, Daimler and Volkswagen had colluded to hold back improvements in vehicle emissions technology.
